rows.grounds: textually uncertain form expressing bodily enjoyment

items.question: How does the belief in a rice-ball giver shape one's imagined afterlife state?
premises: A person imagines having a ritual giver of rice-balls.
Through the sequence of rice-ball offerings, one imagines obtaining bodily enjoyment.
This imagined ritual support produces the sense of being complete and well-established.
items.inference: The conviction of ritual support generates a corresponding experience of bodily completeness in the afterlife imagination.
uncertainties: The token prapnobh/m(?)yavayavābhogaṃ is textually uncertain in the source.
items.plain_english: One thinks, 'Today I have someone to offer me rice-balls; through that offering I enjoy my limbs again, and I am whole and well-established.'

items.question: What heavenly condition is imagined through unseen rites performed by others?
premises: Unseen ritual actions are imagined as performed by sons, disciples, oneself, or others.
These actions are believed to secure a share in heaven.
The result is imagined as complete enjoyment and stable well-being.
items.inference: Belief in unseen rites performed by related agents produces the conviction of a stable and pleasurable heavenly state.
items.plain_english: Through unseen rites arranged by a son, disciple, oneself, or others, one imagines having a share in heaven, fully enjoying it and firmly settled there.

items.question: What fearful afterlife is imagined when ritual support and rescue are absent?
premises: A person imagines having no one to offer rice-balls.
The same person judges himself to be a great wrongdoer with no savior anywhere.
This conviction leads to the imagination of falling into a hellish ocean.
items.inference: The absence of imagined ritual and moral support produces a corresponding vision of helpless descent into hell.
items.plain_english: One thinks, 'I have no one to offer me rice-balls, I myself have done great wrong, there is no savior for me anywhere, and I am falling into the ocean of hell.'

items.question: How do such hopes and fears in awareness come to fruition?
premises: Thoughts arise such as the hope that a savior will appear somewhere and sometime.
These are expansions of cognition, not merely external events.
The expansion of cognition bears fruit in a corresponding way.
items.inference: Cognitive expansions, whether hopeful or fearful, actualize themselves as corresponding experiences.
items.plain_english: Thoughts like 'Somehow, sometime, I will have a savior' are expansions of awareness, and they bear fruit in just that form by themselves.

items.question: What happens if no external ritual agent exists for the imagined afterlife?
premises: An external performer of rice-ball rites may not actually exist.
The cognition still flashes forth in a particular form.
The experiencer undergoes the fruit fashioned by that cognition.
items.inference: The experienced afterlife result depends on the form of cognition, not on the presence of an external ritual agent.
items.plain_english: Even if there is no actual person performing the rice-ball rites, one experiences the result exactly as it appears in awareness, fashioned by one's own resolve.

items.question: What can destroy the deeply hardened belief in such afterlife constructions?
premises: The mistaken belief is hardened by doubt like diamond-hard plaster.
Such a fixation cannot be removed by ordinary means.
The fire of Bhairava-awareness alone can burn it completely and instantly.
items.inference: Only the liberating fire of Bhairava-consciousness can uproot the hardened delusion of afterlife constructions.
items.plain_english: This belief, tightly sealed within by the diamond-hard plaster of doubt, is burned away root and all in an instant by the fire of Bhairava alone.

items.question: What realization burns up the entire dream-house of worldly experience?
premises: The world is like a dream-house contained within varied consciousness.
A fire is needed to burn that dream-house.
The realization 'I alone am Śiva' flashes forth as that fire.
items.inference: The identity-realization 'I am Śiva' is the fire that consumes the entire dreamlike world.
items.plain_english: The fire that burns up the whole dream-house of the world, contained in all varied consciousness, is the flashing realization, 'I alone am Śiva.'

items.question: Why does the deluded person take the varied world-cycle as real?
premises: A deluded person's consciousness is variegated by karmic cognitions.
What appears is fundamentally a construction of resolve.
The deluded person mistakes that construction for a real, varied world-cycle.
items.inference: Delusion consists in taking a resolve-constructed world, shaped by karmic cognition, to be objectively real.
items.plain_english: Deluded by that, with consciousness variegated by karmic cognitions, one takes what is really a construction of resolve to be the varied world of transmigration.

items.question: Why might a child who dies be reborn again as an infant?
premises: A child who dies may lack other developed impressions.
Firm worldly impressions may still remain latent.
Rebirth follows the dominant latent impressions.
items.inference: A deceased child without other impressions may be reborn as an infant because firm worldly impressions remain latent.
items.plain_english: For that reason, a child who dies without other impressions, but with firm worldly tendencies lying dormant, would be born again as an infant.

items.question: How do latent impressions unfold again into later stages of life?
premises: Latent impressions continue to operate after rebirth.
Development proceeds through stages such as youth.
The sequence of those impressions drives that progression again.
items.inference: The unfolding of life stages after rebirth follows the sequence of latent impressions.
uncertainties: The tokens tānyau and (?) are textually unclear in the source.
items.plain_english: In that way, by the sequence of those impressions, one reaches youth again and continues according to those same latent tendencies.

items.question: How do impressions lead a being to identify with various transmigrations and even inert states?
premises: Cognition shaped by impressions makes one identify with particular transmigrations.
An impression of inertness can make a being become inert.
Even in that state, association with subtle elements like space and wind continues.
items.inference: Impression-shaped cognition drives identification with transmigratory forms, including states of inertness.
items.plain_english: Through cognition shaped by impressions, one takes various transmigrations to be real; and someone, through the impression of inertness, may even become inert while still associated with space and wind.

items.question: How can a being pass through vegetal and embryonic forms in transmigration?
premises: Association with earth and water can lead to existence as flower and fruit.
When consumed, that existence can pass into the form of seed.
Through that seed-form, the being can return to a womb state.
items.inference: Transmigration can proceed through elemental, vegetal, and reproductive transformations driven by continuing impressions.
items.plain_english: Joined with earth and water, one may become flower and fruit; eaten and transformed into seed, one may come again into the state of a womb.

items.question: Where do the varied cycles of transmigration actually occur?
premises: The being repeatedly takes varied world-cycles to be real.
This taking-to-be-real is driven by dwelling in one's own impressions and tendencies.
The conscious subject in whom this occurs is Śiva.
items.inference: The varied cycles of transmigration occur in the one conscious locus, Śiva, as experiences shaped by impressions.
items.plain_english: Again and again, Śiva, dwelling in his own impressions and tendencies, takes varied worlds of transmigration to be real, all in one and the same place.

items.question: What kinds of experiences does the self-fashioned consciousness undergo?
premises: Consciousness experiences heavens, hells, and other realms.
These experiences are fashioned by its own freedom.
They may appear in earthlike, waterlike, or mixed forms.
items.inference: The realms and forms experienced in transmigration are self-fashioned manifestations of free consciousness.
items.plain_english: It experiences heavens, hells, and other enjoyments fashioned by its own freedom, appearing sometimes as earthy, sometimes as watery, and sometimes as mixed.

items.question: How does awareness appear as worlds and as pleasure or pain?
premises: Awareness shines by its own nature in the form of worlds.
Wherever it becomes fixed, that fixation occurs in that very locus.
From its own impressions it experiences pleasure and other feelings there.
items.inference: World-appearance and felt experience arise from awareness itself through fixation shaped by its own impressions.
items.plain_english: Thus awareness shines by its own nature as made of worlds; wherever it is held, there, from its own impressions, it experiences pleasure and the like.

items.question: Why is the experiencer's world not publicly visible and not ultimately located in space or time?
premises: The experiencer knows, but is not seen by another in that same experiential form.
The experiencer may know others differently.
In ultimate truth, no independent place or time exists to fix these experiences.
items.inference: Experiential worlds are privately constituted in awareness and lack ultimate grounding in independent space or time.
items.plain_english: One knows, but is not seen by another in that same way; one knows others differently. In ultimate truth, there is no place and no time at all.

items.question: Why does the doctrine of difference fail to establish real spatial distinction?
premises: If space itself is taken as the common place, everything would collapse into one place.
If difference is explained by limiting conditions, those conditions still require spatial distinction.
The distinction of limiting conditions would itself depend on further distinction.
items.inference: In a doctrine of difference, spatial distinction cannot be grounded without circular dependence on limiting conditions.
items.plain_english: In the doctrine of difference, if space is the common place, everything would be in one place; but if difference comes from limiting conditions, even those differently placed conditions depend on further difference.

items.question: What kind of difference, if any, can coherently explain distinction?
premises: Spatial difference collapses into mutual dependence.
Mutual dependence cannot establish any real difference of place.
Only difference of intrinsic nature could coherently serve as a differentiator.
items.inference: If difference is to be coherent, it must be intrinsic difference of nature rather than spatial difference.
items.plain_english: Thus, because of mutual dependence, there is no real difference of place; only a difference of intrinsic nature would fit as a true differentiator.

items.question: Why does intrinsic difference also fail in the light of nondual consciousness?
premises: Intrinsic difference was proposed as the only coherent differentiator.
In realities whose nature is one light, such intrinsic difference does not exist.
This has been established by reflective insight, which some lack.
items.inference: Because all is of the nature of one light, intrinsic difference cannot ultimately exist, though this is missed without reflective insight.
items.plain_english: But that intrinsic difference does not exist in things whose nature is one light; this has already been established. Those who lack this reflective insight miss it.

items.question: What happens to those who lack reflective insight into nondual consciousness?
premises: Some people lack the reflective vision that sees the one light.
They are made doubtful by floods of scriptures that generate doubt.
They become absorbed in constructions imagined like inert beings in their own dreams.
items.inference: Without reflective insight, people are overwhelmed by doubt-producing scriptural constructions and become identified with dreamlike projections.
items.plain_english: Those deprived of that insight are made doubtful by floods of doubt-producing scriptures and become absorbed in them, taking as real the endless inert beings imagined in their own dreams.

items.question: Why do seeming scriptures create doubt in those without awakening?
premises: Those devoid of awakening are made to grasp doubt by seeming scriptures.
This doubt is ultimately futile.
Awareness may remain hidden for long but can still awaken.
items.inference: Seeming scriptures only trouble those lacking awakening, while awareness itself can awaken even after long latency.
items.plain_english: Those without awakening are vainly made to cling to doubt by mere semblances of scripture; yet awareness, though hidden for long, can still awaken.

items.question: Why do mental constructions still seem to bear fruit in experience?
premises: Mental constructions and similar projections appear to bear fruit.
This happens mostly through constructions of mind and related faculties.
Underlying them is the sovereignty of freedom that manifests multiplicity.
items.inference: Mental constructions bear experiential fruit because consciousness freely manifests multiplicity through them.
items.plain_english: Even so, such things mostly bear fruit through constructions of the mind and the like, because of the sovereign freedom that manifests multiplicity.

items.question: How does a fashioned appearance become an embodied experience of disturbance?
premises: Whatever is fashioned in awareness becomes that experiencer's embodied form.
This can occur under the influence of reversed or distorted appearances.
Such distortion may be tainted by sensations like cold and others.
items.inference: A mentally fashioned appearance can manifest as an embodied condition, especially when distorted by adverse sensations.
items.plain_english: Whatever is fashioned becomes for that person a body and the like; when joined with reversed appearances and tainted by sensations such as cold, it takes that disturbed form.

items.question: How is bodily disturbance described when the body's vital mechanism is altered?
premises: The subtle channels and related bodily structures can be afflicted.
The body is likened to a great bellows-machine driven by the wheel of vital winds.
When this mechanism goes awry, contraction, bursting, striking, and similar disturbances arise.
items.inference: Bodily suffering is explained as the malfunction of the body’s wind-driven mechanism affecting its channels.
items.plain_english: Then, when the channels and so forth are afflicted by contraction, bursting, blows, and the like, the body—like a great bellows-machine with its wheel of winds—goes out of order.
